ety.text: Collectively borrowed from Early Modern Spanish zero, Middle French zero, and (their etymon) Old Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zēphirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing; cipher”), itself calqued from Sanskrit शून्य (śūnyá, “void; nothingness”). Doublet of cipher and chiffre. Cognate with Spanish cero and French zéro.

senses.d: The cardinal number occurring before one and that denotes no quantity or amount at all, represented in Arabic numerals as 0.
ex: The conductor waited until the passenger count was zero.
A cheque for zero dollars and zero cents crashed the computers on division by zero.

senses.d: The numeric symbol that represents the cardinal number zero.
ex: In unary and k-adic notation in general, zero is the empty string.
Write 0.0 to indicate a floating point number rather than the integer zero.

senses.d: The digit 0 in the decimal, binary, and all other base numbering systems.
ex: One million has six zeroes.
zero-defect
The shipment was lost, so they had zero in stock.

senses.d: The value of a magnitude corresponding to the cardinal number zero.
ex: The electromagnetic field does not drop all of the way to zero before a reversal.

senses.d: The point on a scale at which numbering or measurement originates.
ex: The temperature outside is ten degrees below zero.

senses.d: A value of the independent variables of a function, for which the function is equal to zero.
ex: The zeroes of a polynomial are its roots by the fundamental theorem of algebra.
The derivative of a continuous, differentiable function that twice crosses the axis must have a zero.

senses.d: The additive identity element of a monoid or greater algebraic structure, particularly a group or ring.
ex: Since a commutative zero is the inverse of any additive identity, it must be unique when it exists.
The zero (of a ring or field) has the property that the product of the zero with any element yields the zero.
They rudely treated him like a zero.

senses.d: A difference that is present at an abstract level, but not realized in the form, that is, superficially (on the surface).
ex: Sometimes a difference in intended meaning has only a zero to mark it, in which case the utterance may be ambiguous when context alone does not fully clarify it.

senses.d: A casual misspelling of Zero ("a fighter aircraft operated by Imperial Japan during World War II").

ex: She showed zero respect.

senses.d: Of a cloud ceiling, limiting vision to 50 feet (15 meters) or less.
Of horizontal visibility, limited to 165 feet (50.3 meters) or less.
Present at an abstract level, but not realized in the surface form.
ex: The stem of "kobieta" with the zero ending is "kobiet".

senses.d: Used in the names of foodstuffs, especially beverages, to indicate a version with no calories
To set some amount to be zero.
ex: They tried to zero the budget by the end of the quarter.
Results were inconsistent because an array wasn’t zeroed during initialization.

senses.d: To disappear or make something disappear.
ex: Traffic on the encrypted channels used by senior Iraqi generals had peaked and zeroed, then peaked again, and zeroed again.
If I zeroed Jack, I'd get by So I'd erased him, pretended the last few months had never happened.

senses.d: To adjust until the variance is reduced to an acceptably low amount.
ex: The soldier took his gun to the shooting range to zero its aim.

point of origin on a scale

ety.text: Borrowed from Italian zero, alteration of zefiro, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صفر. Doublet of chiffre.
Derived from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing”, “cipher”). Doublet of cifra.
Borrowed from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Andalusian Arabic صِفْر (ṣífr), from Classical Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, nothing, empty, void”).
Borrowed from French zéro, from Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing, cipher”). Doublet of cifra.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nada, from Latin (nūlla rēs) nāta (literally “no born thing, not a thing born”).

chain.g: no one, none, not any, nothing

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French nul, from Old French nul, from Latin nūllus.
Proto-Italic *oinosder. Proto-Italic *noinolos Latin nullusbor. Spanish nulo Borrowed from Latin nullus (“none”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese nin (h)ũu, earlier nen (h)ũu, from Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Displaced the collateral form ningũu. Compare Galician ningún, Spanish ninguno.

it:azzerare.gl: to zero, to reset, to clear

pt:zerar.gl: to set a measuring instrument to zero
